Who sets and collects property tax in Massachusetts?

Each of the state's 351 cities and towns assesses and collects its own property tax, so the bill for a house depends on the municipality, not the county. The Division of Local Services, part of the Department of Revenue, oversees the system, and your local board of assessors holds the property record card for your house.

Value is set as of January 1 for the fiscal year that follows. The Appellate Tax Board's guide gives an example: fiscal year 2025 runs July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025, and its valuation date is January 1, 2024. For a seller, that gap explains why a bill can reflect a value set well before you list the house.

What is Proposition 2½ and how does it limit your tax bill?

Proposition 2½ limits what a city or town can raise in total, not what any single owner pays. The Division of Local Services describes two restrictions: the levy cannot exceed 2.5% of the community's total assessed value, and the yearly increase is capped at 2.5% of the prior year's levy limit plus new growth.

Voters can raise the amount above that only through an override, a debt exclusion or a capital exclusion. The same article reports that statewide excess levy capacity was $918 million in fiscal 2025, equal to 3.9% of the levy limit, and that more than half of the municipalities (186) had excess capacity below 1% of the maximum levy.

Individual bills still move, because the total levy is divided among all taxable property. When your neighbors' values rise faster than yours, your share can fall even when your own value goes up.

When are Massachusetts property tax bills due?

Due dates depend on how your municipality bills. In quarterly towns, installments are generally due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. In towns that bill twice a year, a bill is generally due 30 days after it is mailed.

Billing styleGeneral due dates
QuarterlyAugust 1, November 1, February 1, May 1
Twice a yearThirty days from the mailing of the bill

The face of your actual tax bill states the due date for payment and for abatement requests. If a bank or mortgage company pays your tax, the Appellate Tax Board's guide stresses that it is still your responsibility to make sure the payment arrives on time.

How do you apply for an abatement?

You file an abatement application with your local board of assessors on the approved form, on or before the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. In quarterly municipalities that date is generally February 1, and in twice-a-year municipalities it is generally 30 days after the bill is mailed.

  • Forms are available from the local assessors' office.
  • An abatement is a reduction in tax, usually granted when you can show fair cash value is lower than the assessed value. It can also be granted for an exemption or an improper classification.
  • Fair cash value is the price a willing seller and a willing buyer would agree on in an arm's-length sale, with neither under compulsion.
  • The postmark rule treats the postmark date as the filing date for mail sent through the U.S. Postal Service or an approved delivery service.

Assessors have three months to act. They can deny, grant in full or in part, or do nothing, and they must send written notice within ten days of acting. If they do nothing, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, not 90 days.

How do you appeal to the Appellate Tax Board?

You file with the Appellate Tax Board within three months of the assessors' action, or within three months of the deemed denial if they never acted. When the notice shows two dates, count from the date of action, not the mailing date.

Three requirements are jurisdictional, meaning the board cannot hear the case without them: timely payment of the tax, a timely abatement application on the approved form, and a timely appeal. The guide says no exceptions can be made. There is one narrow relief on payment: the board can still hear an appeal if the tax due for the year is $5,000 or less, or if you paid at least the average tax of one of the three prior years.

  • The filing fee depends on assessed value under the board's Schedule of Entry Fees.
  • Most single-family appeals use the informal procedure, which waives most further appeal rights.
  • It usually takes four months to a year to get a hearing, most single-family hearings last one to two hours, and a decision arrives within roughly three months.

What must you prove at the hearing?

You carry the burden. A tax assessment is presumed valid, so you must show that the fair cash value of your house is below the assessed value, as of the January 1 valuation date. Saying that the tax went up 20% generally does not succeed, according to the board's guide.

The guide recommends describing the house in detail, reviewing the assessors' record card, and gathering sales of comparable properties that match on type, location, size, timing and condition, with adjustments for differences. You may also use comparable assessments or hire an expert appraiser. Documents must reach the board and the other side at least seven days before the hearing.

There is one exception to the presumption. If the board set a value for one year and assessors raise it in either of the next two fiscal years, the burden shifts to the assessors to justify the increase.

What happens if property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid property tax or water and sewer charges become a lien, and the city or town can eventually take the house. The Land Court describes the steps: after 30 days unpaid, the municipality can send a demand, and if you do not pay within 14 days, it can record a tax taking at the Registry of Deeds.

  • Six or twelve months later, the holder of the tax title can file a foreclosure complaint in the Land Court.
  • A private party can become the tax title owner, for example by buying bundled tax bills or winning an auction.
  • You can file an answer and ask for a hearing, where you may offer to redeem by paying everything owed or ask for a payment plan.
  • If you do not pay by the date the court sets, the court may enter a judgment of foreclosure, which ends your right to get the property back.

A foreclosed owner may try to recover money if the house was worth more than the debt. That is a reason to deal with a tax taking early, before it reaches the Land Court.

How does tax due affect selling a house in Massachusetts?

A recorded tax taking is a title problem that must be cleared before a clean sale, and paying everything owed ends the city or town's claim before a final foreclosure judgment. Ask the closing attorney how any unpaid tax will be handled at the table.

Before listing, request a payoff figure from the collector's office, check your assessors' record for errors, and note any abatement deadline you may miss by selling. The guide does not cover how a pending abatement transfers at a sale, so ask the assessors' office and your closing attorney.

Frequently asked questions

What is the deadline to file a Massachusetts property tax abatement?

It is the due date of the first installment of the actual tax bill. That is generally February 1 in quarterly-billing towns and about 30 days after mailing in twice-a-year towns. Check the face of your bill.

How long do assessors have to decide an abatement?

Three months. If they do not act, the application is deemed denied after three calendar months, and you then have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Do I have to pay the tax while I appeal?

Generally yes. The Appellate Tax Board needs the tax paid on time to have jurisdiction, with limited exceptions when the tax is $5,000 or less or you paid the average of a prior year.

What does Proposition 2½ limit?

It limits the total levy a municipality can raise. The levy cannot exceed 2.5% of total assessed value, and it can rise by 2.5% of the prior levy limit plus new growth unless voters approve more.

Can the city take my house for unpaid property tax?

Yes. After a demand and 14 days, the city or town can record a tax taking, and a Land Court foreclosure can follow. You can redeem by paying all taxes, interest and fees before a final judgment.

What is the Massachusetts homestead exemption?

The Massachusetts homestead exemption is a legal protection for equity in a primary home, set out in G.L. c. 188. It shields that equity from most creditors up to a set dollar amount, and it comes in two forms: an automatic one and a declared one.

It is not a discount on the yearly property tax bill. The Mass.gov law library sends readers looking for tax exemptions, deferrals and abatements to a separate page on property taxes, and those programs are handled through the local board of assessors. This page deals only with the creditor protection under chapter 188.

How much home equity does Massachusetts protect?

The automatic exemption protects $125,000 of equity without any filing, and a recorded declaration raises the protection to $1,000,000. Both figures are defined in section 1 of the chapter.

KindAmountHow it arises
Automatic homestead exemption$125,000Exists for the owner and family who live in the home or intend to, with no filing (section 4)
Declared homestead exemption$1,000,000Created by a written declaration that is recorded (section 5)
Declared by an elderly or disabled ownerUp to $1,000,000 per personOwner is 62 or older, or disabled; a separate declaration under section 2

For a home owned as joint tenants or tenants by the entirety, the exemption stays whole and unallocated, and the owners together cannot exceed the cap. Where owners are tenants in common or trust beneficiaries, the automatic exemption is divided by ownership share, and the declared exemption is divided among those who live in the home as a principal residence.

Which kinds of property count as a protected home?

The statute defines a home broadly, so most owner-occupied residences qualify. A protected home can be any of these, including the land and accessory structures that go with it:

  • A single-family house.
  • A two- to four-family dwelling.
  • A manufactured home.
  • A residential condominium unit.
  • A residential cooperative unit.

The home must be a principal residence, the place where the owner and family live or intend to live as their main dwelling. The law says no person can hold rights in more than one principal residence. The family counts a spouse and any minor child, and the statute sets "minor child" at age 21 and under.

A federal bankruptcy court decision summarized by the law library also found that using part of a property for business does not by itself remove homestead protection.

How do you file a declaration of homestead in Massachusetts?

You sign a written declaration and record it at the Registry of Deeds for the county where the home sits. Section 5 sets what it must contain.

  • It must be signed and acknowledged under penalty of perjury by each owner who is to benefit.
  • It must identify each owner and any non-titled spouse.
  • It must state that each person named lives in the home or intends to as a principal residence.
  • If a married couple co-owns the home as the principal residence of both, both spouses sign.
  • If the home is in a trust, only the trustee signs.
  • It cannot be created inside the deed that gives the owner title.
  • It should state whether anyone named may be a servicemember, though leaving that out does not void it.

The state filing fee is $35, and the law library notes that a county registry may add its own charge. The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds, for example, lists $36 for a declaration of homestead on recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost, and $35 on the Land Court side. Declarations can be filed by mail with notarized signatures and a check.

What is different for owners over 62 or owners with a disability?

An elderly person is defined as someone 62 or older, and a disabled person is someone with a permanent impairment that would meet Supplemental Security Income standards. These owners can record a separate declaration under section 2.

A disabled owner must record proof with the declaration, either an original or certified Social Security Administration disability award letter or a letter from a registered physician certifying that the federal standard is met. Each person benefited under section 2 gets the declared amount without reduction or sharing among other owners, and separate declarations under sections 2 and 3 can sit on the same home.

What happens to a homestead when the house is sold?

A sale ends the homestead on the house but not the protection for the money. Section 10 lists nine ways a homestead terminates, and a deed is the most common one for sellers.

  • A deed to a non-family member, signed by the owner and by any non-owner spouse or former spouse who lives in the home.
  • A recorded release signed and acknowledged by the owner and that spouse.
  • Abandonment of the home as a principal residence, which ends the rights of the person who left.
  • A new declaration on a different property by the same owner.
  • A deed that states the grantor is unmarried or that the property is not the grantor's home.
  • A divorce judgment that requires conveying the home to the other spouse.

Under section 11, the sale proceeds stay protected until the owner buys another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first. For fire or other casualty damage, protection lasts until repairs are done, another home is acquired, or two years pass, whichever comes first. Living in a trailer or other temporary housing does not count as establishing a principal residence.

Does the homestead protect against a mortgage or a refinance?

Mortgages are treated separately from creditor claims. Section 8 of the chapter deals with prior mortgages and liens, and section 9 with subordination of the homestead to a mortgage executed by all owners. Section 10 adds that nothing in a mortgage or its documents ends a homestead, apart from that subordination. Section 4 allows the automatic exemption to be subordinated to a new loan or line of credit only if the loan is under $20,000, not secured by a recorded document, and signed by all record owners and non-titled spouses with a plain-language waiver.

The law library says a declaration does not have to be filed again after refinancing, and that both spouses may file. It also summarizes a 2021 Appeals Court decision: a creditor may levy on an execution and then hold off collecting until the homestead lapses or the homeowner's equity exceeds the protected amount. In practice, a judgment can still be waiting when a protected home is sold, so it helps to ask the title company or attorney what appears in the record.

What should a Massachusetts seller check about the homestead before closing?

Sellers should confirm whether a declaration is on record and who signed it before they accept a closing date. The law library points to the Secretary of the Commonwealth's list of registries as the way to check whether a declaration is recorded on a property.

  • Look up the property at the registry to see whether a declaration or release is recorded.
  • Find out whether a spouse or former spouse who lives in the home needs to sign the deed or a release.
  • Ask whether any judgment lien or tax lien must be paid at closing.
  • Keep proceeds in a way an attorney can explain, because section 11 protection ends one year after the sale unless a new home is bought sooner.

Homes held in trust or owned by several people can involve more signers, so a real estate attorney should read the paperwork first.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Massachusetts homestead automatic?

Yes, to a degree. Chapter 188, section 4 gives an automatic exemption of $125,000 with no filing, as long as the owner and family live in the home or intend to. Recording a declaration raises the protected amount to $1,000,000.

Does the homestead exemption lower my property tax bill?

No. Chapter 188 protects home equity from creditors. Property tax exemptions and abatements are a separate topic handled by your local board of assessors.

How much does it cost to file a declaration of homestead?

The state fee is $35, and a registry may add its own charge. Norfolk County lists $36 for recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost.

Do I have to refile after refinancing?

No. The Trial Court Law Libraries note that there is no need to re-file after refinancing.

What happens if I sell and buy another home?

Sale proceeds stay protected until you acquire another home to live in or one year after the sale, whichever comes first, under section 11.

Can both spouses file a declaration?

Yes. Section 5 requires both spouses to sign when the home is the principal residence of both and is co-owned by the married couple.

Who has to file a Massachusetts estate tax return?

The personal representative must file Form M-706 when the estate is large enough, and for deaths on or after January 1, 2023 that means a gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts above $2,000,000. For deaths from 2006 through 2022 the trigger was $1,000,000. The Department of Revenue guide, last updated April 23, 2026, states these thresholds and notes that changes in federal estate tax law after December 31, 2000 have no effect on the Massachusetts tax.

The guide also covers people who did not live here. A nonresident who owned or transferred Massachusetts real estate or tangible property has the same filing test, measured against the total worldwide estate, and must send Form M-NRA with the return.

ItemWhat DOR says
Filing threshold, deaths from 2023Gross estate over $2,000,000
Filing threshold, deaths 2006 to 2022Gross estate over $1,000,000
Credit, deaths from 2023$99,600
Return and payment dueNine months after death
Late filing penalty1% per month, up to 25%
Late payment penalty1% per month, up to 25%
Estate Tax Unit phone(617) 887-6930

How is the Massachusetts estate tax calculated?

The state computes its tax from the old federal credit for state death taxes, using the Internal Revenue Code as it stood on December 31, 2000, and then subtracts a $99,600 credit. DOR describes the tax as a transfer tax on the value of the estate before distribution to any beneficiary.

The computation turns on the federal Table B, which the guide reproduces. The adjusted taxable estate is the taxable estate less $60,000, and there is no credit when that figure is $40,000 or less. Marginal rates in the table run from 0.8 percent up to 16 percent, which is the range shown on the state's Tax Rates page.

Two details affect real estate directly:

  • For deaths on or after August 1, 2025, the guide removes the value of real and tangible property located outside Massachusetts from a resident's computation.
  • The guide adds back Massachusetts QTIP assets claimed on a predeceased spouse's return, and the steps for deaths between January 1, 2023 and July 31, 2025 are in a separate set of FAQs.

The final amount cannot fall below zero. The guide does not give worked examples for specific estate sizes, so ask DOR or an estate attorney for a real number.

What is the Massachusetts estate lien and why does it matter for a sale?

A lien automatically arises at death on all real estate the decedent owned, either alone or jointly, and it can stand in the way of a clean sale. DOR states that failing to file Form M-706 blocks the Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Lien, and that a release of lien is necessary to obtain clear title and to sell or transfer the real estate.

When the return must be filed, the certificate is needed for several kinds of real estate:

  • Property owned jointly or as tenants by the entirety.
  • Real estate held in trust.
  • Other real estate outside the probate inventory but included in the gross estate.

It can also be required for probate real estate if a sale is pending and no closing letter has been issued. DOR says that if the return was already filed, you should send a copy of the purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment to speed up the certificate.

What if the estate is below the threshold?

Then the personal representative signs an affidavit and records it at the registry of deeds to release the lien. DOR says the affidavit must be made under the pains and penalties of perjury and must accurately state that the gross estate does not require a Massachusetts estate tax filing. That rule applies to estates of decedents dying on or after January 1, 1997.

DOR does not publish blank affidavits for filing in the registry of deeds, so ask the estate's attorney or the registry what form it accepts.

Can the estate sell the house before the nine-month deadline?

Yes, an estate can sell before the return is due, and DOR has a form for it. If a sale or mortgage is happening sooner than nine months after death, or later than nine months while an approved extension is running, the estate can file Form M-4422, Application for Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Tax Lien, through MassTaxConnect.

The application needs an executed purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment, and DOR lists these attachments:

  • An attested copy of the deed.
  • A copy of the purchase and sale agreement or mortgage commitment.
  • A copy of the letter of authority or the trust document.
  • Payment of the estimated tax due.
  • A copy of the death certificate.

The full Form M-706 is still due within nine months of death or within the extension. Filing and paying through MassTaxConnect speeds up the closing letter and the lien release, while mailed returns to P.O. Box 7023, Boston, MA 02204 can delay both.

What extensions and penalties apply?

Every estate return gets an automatic six-month extension to file if at least 80 percent of the tax finally due is paid by the nine-month date. If the 80 percent is missed, the extension is void and the late filing penalty can apply, and interest runs on unpaid tax from the original due date either way.

A separate extension of time to pay is available on Form M-4768 for undue hardship or reasonable cause. Each request covers up to six months, and DOR may grant up to three years from the original due date in total. Interest keeps accruing during that time. The interest rate changes each quarter, so call the DOR contact center at (617) 887-6367 or (800) 392-6089 in Massachusetts for the current figure.

The personal representative can be held personally liable for tax shown on the return that is not paid, which is a good reason to ask an attorney before distributing money to heirs.

What do heirs owe, and what does a cash sale change?

The DOR guide describes a tax on the estate itself, not a tax that each heir pays separately on receiving a share. The guide does not describe a separate inheritance tax. If you think another state tax applies to your situation, ask DOR directly.

A cash sale does not remove the lien rules. What it does is shorten the time a house sits while the estate sorts out paperwork. If you are the personal representative of a Massachusetts estate and the house needs repairs, we can look at it as-is, and the estate's attorney handles the lien release or the recorded affidavit. Our probate page covers the court steps, and our capital gains page covers the income tax side of the sale.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Massachusetts estate tax exemption in 2026?

A Massachusetts estate tax return is required when the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds $2,000,000, for deaths on or after January 1, 2023. Estates also receive a $99,600 credit.

When is the Massachusetts estate tax due?

Nine months after the date of death. An automatic six-month extension to file applies if at least 80 percent of the tax is paid by the nine-month date.

Do I need a lien release to sell an inherited house in Massachusetts?

If the estate is over the threshold, yes in many cases. DOR says a Certificate Releasing Massachusetts Estate Lien is needed to obtain clear title. Smaller estates use a recorded affidavit that the gross estate does not require a filing.

Can I sell the house before filing the estate tax return?

Yes. If a purchase and sale agreement is signed, the estate can apply on Form M-4422 for the certificate releasing the lien. A completed Form M-706 is still due within nine months or the extension period.

Who do I call with questions about the Massachusetts estate tax?

Call the Estate Tax Unit at (617) 887-6930. For other ways to reach the Department of Revenue, call the contact center at (617) 887-6367, weekdays 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

What are the steps of a Massachusetts eviction once the notice runs out?

Once the days on the notice to quit have passed, the landlord can file a summary process case, and only a judge's order can end the tenancy. Massachusetts sets the sequence through the Court System and the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, which describe it in these steps.

  1. The landlord fills out a summons and complaint and hires a sheriff or constable to deliver it to the tenant.
  2. The landlord files the papers in a District Court or a Housing Court.
  3. The tenant may file a written answer, which costs nothing.
  4. The parties go to court, where the case is dismissed, settled by agreement, or tried.
  5. If the landlord wins, the judge may issue an execution, which is the order that lets the move-out go forward.
  6. A sheriff or constable carries out the removal after written notice.

The Mass.gov pages do not promise a total timeline. Each step depends on the court calendar, so an owner planning a sale should treat any single estimate with caution.

Does a Massachusetts eviction go to District Court or Housing Court?

Either one can hear it. Mass.gov says landlords can file in a District Court or a Housing Court, and that Housing Courts are more familiar with housing law than district or superior court judges.

A tenant can ask to transfer a case into Housing Court, though not the other way around. In a Housing Court case, the first appearance is usually aimed at resolving the dispute through mediation, and the case goes to trial only if that fails. Tenants should expect more than one court date.

The legislature's chapter list also shows how the state organizes these courts. Chapter 185A covers the Housing Court of the City of Boston, chapter 185B covers the Housing Court of the County of Hampden, and chapter 185C covers the statewide Housing Court Department. Which court serves a particular town depends on where the house is, so the clerk's office is the place to confirm.

What happens after a judge rules for the landlord?

A ruling for the landlord starts a short clock rather than an immediate move-out. The tenants' guide lays out the timing, which the table summarizes.

StepTimeDetail
Appeal window10 daysCounted from the date the clerk's office enters judgment
Earliest removal11 days after the final decisionThe landlord can then hire a sheriff or constable
Written notice before removal2 daysWeekends and holidays not counted; the notice names the storage facility
Removal hoursMonday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.Not on a holiday
Window to use the execution3 monthsFrom the court decision
Stay of executionUp to 6 monthsUp to a year for elderly or disabled tenants

A tenant who wants to appeal may first have to pay money owed, such as back rent, though the court can be asked to waive that when it is unaffordable.

A tenant can also ask the judge for a stay of execution, which postpones the move. The tenants' guide says a judge may grant one when the eviction is not the tenant's fault or the tenant shows that no good place to live can be found yet. The guide describes the stay as lasting up to six months in most cases.

Can paying the rent stop an eviction after the judgment?

Yes, in one situation. Mass.gov says the landlord cannot move the tenant out when the eviction is based on nonpayment, the tenant pays all the rent due before the execution is used, and the landlord accepts the payment.

All three conditions must hold together. Because it depends on the landlord accepting the money, a written agreement is the safer way to record what both sides have agreed. A pending RAFT application also blocks an eviction, per the state's tenant guide, and the tenant should tell the court if one has been filed.

What happens to a tenant's belongings and to the house when removal day comes?

If the tenant has not left, the sheriff or constable takes the belongings to a licensed storage facility, and the tenant can be charged for moving and storage. The written notice must give the storage address.

  • A storage facility that holds belongings for six months without payment is allowed to sell them.
  • Only a sheriff or constable can carry out the removal, and only after the 11-day wait.
  • A landlord who locks the tenant out without a judge's order can face penalties under G.L. c. 186, section 14.
  • A tenant who leaves voluntarily before removal avoids the moving and storage fees.

For an owner, the house is not truly vacant until the removal is complete and the property has been checked. Buyers who inspect before closing will see whatever condition it was left in.

What if the tenant moves out owing money?

A landlord can still sue for unpaid rent or other damages after the tenant leaves, in either a civil case or small claims. The Court System guide says small claims generally caps recovery at $7,000, so a $9,000 debt would be cut to $7,000 and the other $2,000 waived.

The guide recommends talking to a lawyer before filing a civil action for damages. It also notes a special rule in G.L. c. 139, section 19: if illegal drugs were found in the unit, the landlord can ask for a speedy trial, and the court may order judgment and execution to issue immediately after trial or default.

How does an eviction case affect a house sale in Massachusetts?

An eviction case adds waiting time and paperwork to a sale, and it can follow the people involved for years. Mass.gov says a case can appear on a tenant's housing record and a money judgment can affect credit, though a tenant may ask to seal the record or file a satisfaction of judgment once paid.

For owners, the practical effects tend to be these:

  • Possession cannot be promised on a fixed date until the court process and the removal are done.
  • A landlord has three months to use an execution, so timing matters if the house is under contract.
  • A tenant in the middle of a case may stay until removal, which affects showings and inspections.
  • Back rent and court costs are separate from the sale and are not wiped out by it.

Owners who would rather skip the court calendar sometimes sell with the tenant in place, or negotiate a move-out date in writing. A real estate attorney can say which path fits a particular lease or tenancy at will.

Where can landlords and tenants get free help during an eviction?

The state runs several free resources. The Community Mediation Centers offer free pre-court mediation, the Court Service Centers help court users without lawyers regardless of income or immigration status, and the Legal Resource Finder points to legal aid programs.

Tenants behind on rent can apply to RAFT through their regional administering agency. Landlords can start an application too, which the tenants' guide notes is useful because the program needs the landlord's cooperation.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an eviction take in Massachusetts?

The state guides do not give a total, because it depends on the notice period, the court calendar and the time for appeal and removal. After judgment, the earliest removal is 11 days after the final decision.

Can a landlord evict a tenant without going to court in Massachusetts?

No. A landlord cannot lock a tenant out or remove them without a judge's order, and doing so can bring penalties under G.L. c. 186, section 14.

How long does a landlord have to use an execution?

Three months from the court decision. The execution is only valid for that window.

Can a tenant be evicted while a RAFT application is pending?

No, according to the Mass.gov tenants' guide, which says a tenant cannot be evicted while a RAFT application is pending and should tell the court about it.

Who serves the eviction papers?

An authorized constable or sheriff must serve the summons and complaint. The landlord cannot serve them personally.

What if the tenant moves out before the court date?

The landlord can still sue for unpaid rent or damages, in small claims for up to $7,000 or in a civil action for more.

What does a quitclaim deed do in Massachusetts?

A Massachusetts quitclaim deed conveys whatever interest the grantor can lawfully convey. Chapter 183, section 2 of the General Laws says a deed of quitclaim and release is sufficient to convey all the estate that could lawfully be conveyed by a deed of bargain and sale.

The state also defines the covenants that go with it. The words quitclaim covenants, or limited covenants, mean the grantor promises the property is free of encumbrances made by the grantor, and will defend the title against claims by, through or under the grantor, but against no one else. That is narrower than a promise about the whole history of the title.

How does a quitclaim deed differ from a warranty deed?

The difference is the scope of the grantor's promises. A quitclaim deed with quitclaim covenants limits the guarantee to the grantor's own acts, while Massachusetts also provides a statutory form for a warranty deed with broader warranty covenants.

ItemQuitclaim covenants
StatuteM.G.L. c. 183, section 17
Free of encumbrancesOnly those made by the grantor
Defends title againstClaims by, through or under the grantor
Claims from earlier ownersNot covered

A buyer who accepts a quitclaim deed is relying on the grantor's own acts only, so ask your closing attorney what extra title work is wise.

What must a Massachusetts deed contain before the registry will record it?

Every deed presented for record must contain, or have endorsed on it, the full name, residence and post office address of the grantee, and a recital of the full consideration. Section 6 of chapter 183 sets this out.

  • Full consideration means the total price without deduction for liens or encumbrances the grantee assumes or that remain.
  • If the deed is not for a specific sum of money, it must state the nature of the other consideration.
  • The endorsements and recitals are recorded as part of the deed.
  • No register of deeds may accept a deed that does not comply, although failure does not affect the deed's validity.

This is why a quitclaim deed used for a gift or a family transfer still needs a stated consideration. An incomplete deed can be rejected at the counter and delay a closing.

Where is a Massachusetts deed recorded?

Deeds are recorded at the county Registry of Deeds, and Massachusetts has two title systems. Recorded land is filed in the registries, and registered land is held by the Land Court in registered land districts housed within the registries.

According to the Trial Court Law Libraries, deeds to 80 to 90 percent of properties are filed as recorded land. Registers stamp each recorded document with a book and page number, and the documents are available online at masslandrecords.com. Registered land is described on a Certificate of Title, which is treated as a Land Court decree, so a deed for registered land goes through the Land Court side of the registry.

Before you sign, find out which system your property is in. The Registry's staff can tell you, and so can the existing deed at masslandrecords.com.

How much is the deeds excise tax?

The state statute sets the deeds excise tax at $2 for each $500, or fraction, of consideration, and $1.50 in Barnstable County. Chapter 64D, section 1 says no tax applies to an instrument given to secure a debt or to a deed where the commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States is a party.

Registries post the current figure. The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds lists an excise tax of $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction of the consideration stated on the deed, and gives an example: a deed with $155,000 consideration requires $706.80. It says no excise tax is due where consideration is less than $100.

  • The tax is paid when the deed is recorded.
  • Norfolk requires a separate attorney's check or bank check for the excise tax.
  • A second check covers the recording fees.

Ask the registry for your county's current rate and payment rules, since the statute figure and the registry's posted amount are not the same.

What are recording fees for a deed?

Fees vary by registry. Norfolk's schedule lists a $156 fee for a deed on recorded land, including a $1 mailing cost, and $155 on the Land Court side. The same schedule lists $36 for a declaration of homestead and $256 for a declaration of trust.

Norfolk's page also says the $1 postage and document return charge does not apply to documents filed electronically as of July 1, 2025. If a document must be recorded in both the Land Court and the registry, a separate check is required for each. Other counties publish their own schedules, so confirm with the registry that will record your deed.

Do home inspections affect a Massachusetts sale?

Yes, for certain residential properties. The Trial Court Law Libraries point to 760 CMR 74, which says sellers of those properties will not condition acceptance of an offer on the waiver of a home inspection, and will not accept offers from buyers who have said they intend to waive one.

The same page notes that closings of the types of transactions in one Supreme Judicial Court decision require the substantive participation of an attorney on behalf of the mortgage lender. Whatever the deed form, expect an attorney to be part of the closing, and ask yours early which documents they will prepare.

Does a quitclaim deed fix title problems?

No. A quitclaim deed passes what the grantor owns, and it cannot cure a defect that already exists. A deed on its own does not show liens, tax takings or probate gaps, so ask an attorney what title work to do.

The Trial Court Law Libraries note that real estate attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling in Massachusetts, by law and practice. A lender's attorney must also certify title on certain purchase money mortgages for dwellings of up to four families under M.G.L. c. 93, section 70.

  • Check for unpaid property tax or a recorded tax taking.
  • Confirm who must sign, including any co-owner or estate representative.
  • Confirm whether the land is recorded or registered.
  • Review the deed form with a Massachusetts attorney.

When does a quitclaim deed work for a sale?

It works when the grantor holds clear title and the buyer is comfortable with limited covenants and a title search. It is a common instrument for sales and for family transfers.

A seller of a one or two family home also needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet sale requirements, and the Department of Fire Services advises calling as soon as you have a closing date. If the owner has died, the deed must come from a personal representative with authority to sell. Do not use a quitclaim deed to move a house out of a probate estate unless a lawyer confirms the steps.

Yes. Chapter 183, section 2 says a deed of quitclaim and release is sufficient to convey all the estate that could lawfully be conveyed by a deed of bargain and sale.

What does the grantee information on a deed have to include?

The grantee's full name, residence and post office address, plus a recital of the full consideration. The register of deeds may not accept a deed that lacks them.

The statute sets $2 for each $500 or fraction of consideration, and the Norfolk County Registry posts $2.28 per $500. Confirm the current rate with the registry where you record.

At the county Registry of Deeds for recorded land, or through the Land Court side of the registry for registered land. Each recorded document is stamped with a book and page number.

Does Massachusetts have a transfer on death deed?

The official pages we opened do not describe a statutory transfer on death deed form for Massachusetts real estate, and we are not going to guess. Before you rely on any deed that is supposed to pass a house at death, have a Massachusetts attorney confirm in writing that it works and how it is recorded.

What the sources do say is more limited. The Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code, in G.L. c. 190B, section 6-101, says a provision for a nonprobate transfer on death in a long list of instruments is nontestamentary. The list includes insurance policies, accounts, securities, trusts, and a conveyance or deed of gift, along with any other written instrument effective as a contract, gift, conveyance or trust.

That section is general. It tells you such provisions are not wills, but it does not by itself create a specific deed form for a house. The Legislature's chapter list also shows a separate chapter 201E, the Uniform Transfer on Death Security Registration Act, which by its title concerns securities rather than land.

What happens to a house when the owner dies?

It depends on how title is held. The Probate and Family Court explains that whether an estate has to be probated depends on how the decedent's property is titled when they die.

Some property passes directly by law and stays out of the probate estate. The court's page names three examples. Jointly held property with a right of survivorship goes to the surviving owner, proceeds from a life insurance policy or an account that names a beneficiary go to that beneficiary, and property held in a trust created by the decedent is handled under the trust.

Typically you must probate the estate if you need to change the title of real estate that is only in the decedent's name without any right of survivorship. A house titled solely to the person who died is the standard case, and it is why this question matters to heirs who want to sell.

  • Sole owner, no survivorship, no trust: probate is usually needed to change title.
  • Joint owners with survivorship: the survivor takes by law.
  • House held in the decedent's trust: the trust terms and trustee control.

What are the types of probate in Massachusetts?

Massachusetts has three types of probate and a simplified process called voluntary administration, according to the Probate and Family Court. Which one fits depends on the will, the heirs and whether the estate includes land.

ProcessKey points from the court's page
Informal probateAdministrative, handled by a Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code magistrate with no hearings. A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after death. Requires the original will, the official death certificate, and the identity and location of all heirs and devisees.
Formal probateTypically heard by a judge and may involve hearings. Used to object to an informal probate, when the will is a copy or has handwritten changes, when its terms are unclear, or when supervised administration is needed.
Late and limited formal probateFor deaths on or after March 31, 2012, when no proceeding happened within 3 years and only confirmation of ownership of probate assets is needed. The personal representative cannot get a license to sell the decedent's real estate.
Voluntary administrationFor estates that consist entirely of personal property worth $25,000 or less, excluding a car, with no real estate.

A house takes an estate out of voluntary administration, since that process is described as being for an estate with few assets and no real estate.

Is there a deadline to probate an estate?

The general rule is three years from the date of death. The Probate and Family Court's page on when probate is necessary says an estate has to be probated within 3 years of when the decedent died.

The deadline does not apply to a voluntary administration, to determining heirs, or to an ancillary proceeding. If the decedent died on or after March 31, 2012 and nothing was filed within the three years, a late and limited formal probate may be available, and in some cases voluntary administration too if its criteria are met.

That late route has a catch for anyone hoping to sell. Because a late and limited personal representative cannot get a license to sell real estate, an heir who waited past three years may have a harder path to a clean sale than one who started early. Talk to a probate attorney about your timeline.

  • Within 3 years: full set of probate options available.
  • After 3 years: late and limited formal probate for deaths on or after March 31, 2012.
  • Voluntary administration: at least 30 days must have passed since death, and the estate must meet the personal property limit.

Who can serve as personal representative?

A person with legal priority, usually the executor named in the will. The court's page says that if the decedent left a will, the person with legal priority is the person named in the will as personal representative or executor.

If there was no will, the surviving spouse has priority. If the decedent was not married when they died, the decedent's heirs have priority. A qualified person with priority has the right to be appointed over anyone else.

The personal representative is the person who collects, manages and transfers estate property to the devisees or heirs. When a house is part of the estate, they are also who will sign the sale paperwork, subject to whatever authority the court gives. Informal probate requires that the person to be appointed has priority.

How does recording fit in when an inherited house is sold?

A sale deed from the estate or its representative is recorded at the registry of deeds like any other. G.L. c. 183, section 4 provides that a conveyance of a fee simple estate is not valid against most outside parties unless recorded in the registry for the county or district where the land lies.

Ask your probate attorney what proof of authority the registry for your county requires from the person signing for the seller. Chapter 202 of the General Laws, which by its title covers sales, mortgages and leases of real estate by executors, administrators, guardians and conservators, is the part of the code to ask about.

  • Probate the estate if the house was in the decedent's sole name.
  • Confirm the personal representative's authority to sell.
  • Close with an attorney and record the deed at the registry for the property's county.

Heirs who inherit a house they do not want to keep can sell it as-is. Cash Home Buyers can give an offer on an inherited Massachusetts house, and your attorney should confirm the estate paperwork is in order before closing.

What should you ask a Massachusetts attorney?

Ask whether any deed on your property transfers it at death, who the sole owner is, and what process the estate would need. Bring your current deed and any trust or will.

  • How is title held on my house today?
  • If I die, would the house need probate?
  • Would a trust or joint ownership with survivorship fit my family and my goals?

It is a deed that names who receives property when the owner dies.

Does a house always go through probate in Massachusetts?

No. The Probate and Family Court says it depends on how the property is titled. Jointly held property with survivorship, property in a trust, and accounts naming beneficiaries can pass outside probate.

What is the deadline to probate an estate in Massachusetts?

The general rule is 3 years from the date of death. A late and limited formal probate may be available for deaths on or after March 31, 2012, but that route cannot license a sale of real estate.

Can voluntary administration be used for an estate with a house?

No. The court describes voluntary administration as for estates with no real estate and personal property worth $25,000 or less, excluding a car.

How fast can informal probate start?

A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after death, if you have the original will, the death certificate and the identity of all heirs and devisees.

What are the types of probate in Massachusetts?

Massachusetts has three types of probate plus a simplified process called voluntary administration. The Probate and Family Court lists them as informal probate, formal probate, and late and limited formal probate.

TypeWho decidesMain feature
Informal probateA Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code magistrateAdministrative, no hearings
Formal probateUsually a judgeOne or more court hearings
Late and limited formal probateThe courtFor estates with no proceeding within 3 years
Voluntary administrationThe court, simplifiedSmall estate, no real estate

For a family that wants to sell an inherited house, the type of proceeding decides how soon a sale can close, so it is worth choosing early.

When can you use informal probate?

Informal probate is available only if you meet all the requirements, and it can be faster. A magistrate can issue an informal order as early as 7 days after the death.

  • You have the original will, if there is one, and the official death certificate.
  • You know the identity and location of all heirs and devisees.
  • The person to be appointed personal representative has priority for appointment.
  • Any incapacitated or minor spouse, heir or devisee is represented by a conservator or a guardian who is not the person filing.
  • The court has not required supervised administration.
  • No judge needs to sign an order or final decree.

You must deliver written notice to the people entitled to it at least 7 days before filing. The court's filing fee for an informal petition is $375, plus a $15 surcharge, and you can file online, by mail or in person in the county where the decedent lived. After the court accepts the petition, post a publication notice within 30 days in a newspaper the register designates.

When do you need formal probate?

You file a formal probate when informal probate is not available or when a judge must act. The court lists several reasons that apply to families holding a house.

  • Someone objects to an informal probate.
  • The will is a copy, or has handwritten words added or crossed out.
  • The terms of the will are unclear.
  • A special personal representative is needed.
  • An incapacitated person or minor heir needs representation.
  • The person asking to serve does not have priority, or is a creditor or public administrator.

Formal matters usually involve one or more hearings before a judge, so plan for a longer timeline than with informal probate. Supervised administration, where the court approves each step, is possible but the court says it is not commonly required.

Who can sell a house the decedent owned?

A personal representative can sell estate real estate to an arm's-length third party, but only if one of two conditions is met. Section 3-715 of the Massachusetts Uniform Probate Code, chapter 190B, covers this power, and it applies whether the representative was appointed formally or informally.

  • If the person died without a will, a license to sell must have been issued under chapter 202.
  • If the person died with a will, either the will, probated formally or informally, gave the representative power to sell that real estate, or a chapter 202 license has been issued.

When those conditions are met, the sale is conclusive even if someone later contests the informal probate. Keep the appointment and the will language or license together so your closing attorney can review them.

Can a late and limited appointment sell the house?

No. The court states that a personal representative appointed in a late and limited formal probate cannot get a license to sell the decedent's real estate. That appointment can only confirm ownership of probate assets in the successors and pay administration expenses.

This type applies when the decedent died on or after March 31, 2012, no original estate proceeding happened within 3 years of the death, and you only need a formal proceeding to confirm ownership. If an old house has sat for years, you may need a different route if a sale is the goal, and a probate attorney can tell you which.

What if the owner lived outside Massachusetts?

You file in any Massachusetts county where the decedent had property when they died. The court's instructions say that if the person did not live in Massachusetts, you may also need to file additional forms in the state where they lived.

An ancillary proceeding like this also needs an authenticated copy of the will, if there is one, and of the appointment. If the person lived in Massachusetts, the rule is simpler: file in the county where they lived at death.

You can check the status of a case online and file through the court's eFiling system. Contact the Probate and Family Court location for the county before you travel, because accepted payment methods for fees vary.

What is voluntary administration and does it cover a house?

Voluntary administration is for estates with few assets and no real estate. It requires a Massachusetts resident decedent whose estate consists entirely of personal property worth $25,000 or less, not counting a car, and at least 30 days since the death.

Because a house is real estate, an estate that includes one cannot use this process. Another probate proceeding also cannot be pending. A voluntary personal representative's authority is limited and does not lead to an official court appointment, which is why a house sale calls for one of the other types.

What forms does an informal probate petition need?

The forms depend on whether there is a will. For a will, the court's page lists the petition (MPC 150), the surviving spouse, children and heirs form (MPC 162), the devisees form (MPC 163), the original will, a certified death certificate, a notice and return of service (MPC 550), a proposed order (MPC 750) and a publication notice (MPC 551).

Without a will, you file the same petition, heirs form, death certificate and notice, plus a bond (MPC 801). You may need a military affidavit if not every interested party agrees, and proof of any guardianship or conservatorship. The court also offers a checklist for informal probate, MPC 966, which is worth reading before you file.

How can an inherited house be sold quickly?

The sale can close as soon as the personal representative has authority to sell and the title is clear. Heirs who live out of state, or who do not want to repair and clean the house, sometimes choose a buyer who purchases as-is, with the appointment and license or will language handed to the closing attorney.

Property tax, utilities and insurance continue during probate, so keep them current to avoid a tax taking. If you are unsure whether you need informal or formal probate, contact the Probate and Family Court in the county where the person lived, or a Massachusetts probate attorney.

Cash Home Buyers in Massachusetts

Does Massachusetts tax the gain when I sell a house?

Yes, the gain can be taxed as income, but an owner who sells a main home may be able to keep a large part of it out of the calculation. The pages we reviewed treat the profit as income on your state return, and the Department of Revenue sets the rate by how long you held the property.

The same return reports everything else you earned that year, so a large sale can sit next to other income near the surtax threshold. It is worth asking a preparer about timing before you sign.

Type of gainMassachusetts rate
Long-term capital gain5.00%
Short-term capital gain8.5%
Long-term gain on collectibles12.00%, with a 50% deduction
Extra surtax, tax year 20264% on income over $1,107,750
Extra surtax, tax year 20254% on income over $1,083,150
Extra surtax, tax year 20244% on income over $1,053,750

The rates come from the state's Tax Rates page, last updated December 30, 2025. A house is not a collectible, so the 12 percent line matters only for items sold alongside a property.

How does the principal residence exclusion work in Massachusetts?

Massachusetts follows the federal rule that lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of a principal residence, or $500,000 if you file jointly. The state's own budget document describes this as conformity to Internal Revenue Code section 121 and cites M.G.L. c. 62, sections 1(c), 1(d) and 2(a).

The Governor's FY25 tax expenditure budget estimated this exclusion at $435.5 million for FY2025, up from $359.3 million in FY2021. The figure shows the exclusion is a sizable item in the state budget.

  • It applies to a principal residence, so an investment property or a second home does not qualify.
  • The dollar caps are $250,000 for one filer and $500,000 for joint filers.
  • Any gain above the cap is taxed at the rate that fits the holding period.

Confirm the federal qualification tests with a tax professional before you rely on the exclusion.

What is different about an investment house or a rental?

A rental house you sell does not get the principal residence exclusion, so the whole gain is exposed to the 5 percent or 8.5 percent rate. The exclusion is written for a principal residence, and the state budget entry says nothing about rentals. If you are selling a tenant-occupied house, the rate depends on your holding period.

Investors who hold a house for more than one year get the lower long-term rate in the state's rate table, which the Department of Revenue describes as applying to long-term gains, while gains on assets held a year or less fall in the 8.5 percent group. An investor planning a sale near the one-year mark should check the exact dates with a tax adviser, because the rate difference is 3.5 percentage points on every taxable dollar.

When does Massachusetts want the tax paid on a house sale?

The tax is due with your annual return, and the state's due-dates page sets April 15 as the deadline for the prior year. The 2025 Form 1 was due on or before April 15, 2026. If you sell in the middle of a year and owe a large amount, estimated payments also come into play.

The Department of Revenue lists these 2026 installments on Form 1-ES:

  • April 15, 2026
  • June 16, 2026
  • September 15, 2026
  • January 15, 2027

An extension gives more time to file, not more time to pay, so interest runs on any unpaid amount. To be valid, at least 80 percent of the liability must be paid by the original due date, and a payment of $5,000 or more with an extension must be made electronically. Filing an extension with the IRS does not count as a Massachusetts extension. The department's contact center is (617) 887-6367, or (800) 392-6089 in Massachusetts, weekdays 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Is the deeds excise the same as a capital gains tax?

No. The deeds excise is a transfer tax on the sales price, and the capital gains tax is an income tax on your profit. The Department of Revenue lists the deeds excise at $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed.

As a simple illustration of the math, a $500,000 sale with no assumed mortgage has 1,000 units of $500, and at $2.28 each the excise comes to $2,280. That is an example of arithmetic, not a quote for your sale, and you should ask your closing attorney what applies to your deed. Even if your capital gain is fully excluded, the excise on the deed is a separate line. The Department of Revenue page also points readers to TIR 19-14 for surcharge information.

What other Massachusetts steps affect the net from a sale?

A few state rules can change the closing date and your costs, whatever your tax picture looks like. The Trial Court Law Libraries say attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling by law and by practice. They also explain that deeds to 80 to 90 percent of properties are filed as recorded land at a county Registry of Deeds, while the rest is registered land documented by a Land Court certificate. The Secretary of the Commonwealth runs a service that emails you when a new document is recorded against your property, and deeds can be searched at masslandrecords.com.

Selling a home also requires a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate of compliance from the local fire department, for which the department charges a fee. The Department of Fire Services says to schedule the inspection as soon as you have a closing date. Battery-powered smoke alarms that are more than ten years old or expired must be replaced with 10-year sealed, photoelectric units that have a hush feature.

Property tax is also a separate matter from income tax. In Boston the residential rate is $12.40 per $1,000, and in Cambridge the FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000, according to each city's own page. Those bills are separate from the gain.

What if I inherited the house and want to sell?

An inherited house may carry a different set of questions, and the Massachusetts estate lien and release rules can also affect the closing. Read our Massachusetts estate tax page for the $2,000,000 threshold, the $99,600 credit and the release of lien process, and our probate page for the court side.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Massachusetts capital gains tax rate on a house?

Long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent and short-term gains at 8.5 percent, according to the Department of Revenue. A 4 percent surtax applies to income over $1,107,750 in tax year 2026.

How much gain can I exclude when I sell my main home in Massachusetts?

Up to $250,000, or $500,000 if you file jointly. Massachusetts conforms to Internal Revenue Code section 121 for this exclusion, per the state's tax expenditure budget.

Is there a difference between short-term and long-term gains on a house?

Yes. Gains on assets held one year or less are taxed at 8.5 percent, while long-term gains are taxed at 5.00 percent. The difference is 3.5 percentage points on the taxable amount.

Do I owe the deeds excise even if my gain is excluded?

Yes, the deeds excise is a separate transfer tax. The state lists it at $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed. Ask your closing attorney for the figure on your sale.

When do I pay Massachusetts tax on the gain?

With your annual return, due April 15 of the following year. For large gains, estimated payments on Form 1-ES may apply, and an extension to file does not extend the time to pay.

Where is a Massachusetts deed recorded?

A deed to Massachusetts land is recorded at the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the land lies. That location rule comes from G.L. c. 183, section 4, which says a conveyance of a fee simple estate is not valid against most outside parties unless it is recorded in the registry for the county or district where the land is.

The same section carves out a few people who are bound anyway: the grantor, the grantor's heirs and devisees, and anyone with actual notice of the deed. In practice that means a buyer should never leave a signed deed in a drawer. Until it is recorded, a later buyer, a creditor or an attachment could win a priority fight against it.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. Whoever closes the sale, usually an attorney for the buyer or the buyer's lender, takes the deed to the right registry after the funds move. You do not file it yourself, but you should know where it goes and how to confirm it landed.

What are recorded land and registered land?

Massachusetts runs two title systems side by side: recorded land and registered land. The Trial Court Law Libraries conveyancing page explains that deeds to eighty to ninety percent of the properties in the Commonwealth are filed as recorded land.

Recorded land works the way most people picture it. The registry stamps each document with a book and page number, and the documents are available online. Registered land is different. Its ownership is described on a Certificate of Title, which the law library calls a decree issued by the Land Court, listing the owner, the land description and any encumbrances.

Registered land is still handled at the county registry, because the Land Court's registered land districts are housed inside the county registries. It does change what you file. The Norfolk County registry, for example, publishes two columns on its fee schedule, one for recorded land and one for the Land Court side, and notes that a document needing both needs two separate checks.

  • Recorded land: indexed by book and page, searchable online.
  • Registered land: tied to a Certificate of Title issued through the Land Court.
  • Not sure which you have: ask your closing attorney or the registry.

What must a Massachusetts deed contain to be accepted for recording?

A deed presented for record must carry the grantee's full name, residence and post office address, plus a recital of the full consideration. That is the rule in G.L. c. 183, section 6.

The statute defines full consideration as the total price for the conveyance, without deducting any liens or encumbrances the grantee assumes or that remain on the property. If the deed is not given for a set sum of money, it must describe the nature of the other consideration instead. Those endorsements and recitals are recorded as part of the deed.

One detail surprises sellers. The same section says failure to comply does not affect the validity of the deed, yet a register of deeds may not accept a non-compliant deed for recording. A deed can be perfectly good between the parties and still bounce at the counter.

  • Grantee's full legal name and mailing address on the deed or endorsed on it.
  • The stated price in dollars, measured before subtracting a mortgage the buyer takes over.

How much does recording a deed cost in Massachusetts?

Recording costs two separate items: a registry recording fee and the deeds excise tax. Fees are set and posted by each registry, so the safest figure is the one on your own registry's current schedule.

As one concrete example, the Norfolk County Registry of Deeds fee schedule lists a deed at $156.00 for recorded land and $155.00 on the Land Court side. The same page shows a mortgage at $206.00, a mortgage discharge at $106.00 per marginal reference, a declaration of homestead at $36.00 and a municipal lien certificate at $81.00. The registry adds a one dollar postage and document return charge for documents mailed or recorded in person, and as of July 1, 2025 that charge does not apply to electronic filings.

Item (Norfolk County registry schedule)Recorded landLand Court side
Deed$156.00$155.00
Mortgage$206.00$205.00
Mortgage discharge$106.00$105.00
Declaration of homestead$36.00$35.00
Copies, per page$1.00$1.00

Other registries publish their own schedules, so a deed recorded in a different county may cost a different amount. Ask the registry or your attorney for the number that applies.

How does the Massachusetts deeds excise tax work?

The deeds excise tax is charged on the consideration stated in the deed, per $500 or fraction of $500. The base rate in G.L. c. 64D, section 1 is $2.00 for each additional $500 or fractional part, and in Barnstable County the same section sets $1.50.

The statute applies to deeds where the consideration, not counting liens or encumbrances that remain, exceeds one hundred dollars. It does not apply to an instrument given to secure a debt, or to a deed where the Commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States or their agencies are a party.

The Norfolk County registry states the amount it collects as $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction, and works an example: a $155,000 deed requires $706.80 in excise tax. I could not reconcile the statute's base figure with the registry's posted rate from the pages I opened, so treat the registry's current schedule as the number to pay. The registry also says the excise tax must be paid by an attorney's check or a bank check, separate from the recording fee, and that no tax is due where consideration is under $100.

  • The tax is computed from the price on the deed, so the stated consideration matters.
  • Who pays the tax is a term of the purchase agreement, so confirm it with your attorney before you sign.
  • A fractional $500 counts as a full $500, so the amount rounds up.

What do you bring or send to the registry of deeds?

You send the original signed deed, the recording fee and the excise tax payment, along with whatever else your registry asks for.

Because lenders and title insurers usually insist on it, the closing attorney typically handles all of this. In its summary of the law, the Trial Court Law Libraries page notes that attorneys are a regular part of buying and selling real estate in Massachusetts, by law and practice, and cites the Supreme Judicial Court's decision in Real Estate Bar Association v. National Real Estate Information Services, 459 Mass. 512 (2011), which held that a lender's closing requires an attorney's substantive participation.

  • The signed, acknowledged original deed, not a photocopy.
  • A check or electronic payment for the recording fee, payable as the registry directs.
  • A separate bank or attorney's check for the excise tax.

Norfolk County states it takes cash or check for recording and copy fees and wants a separate check for each side if a document must be recorded in both the Land Court and the registry.

How can a seller check that a Massachusetts deed was recorded?

Search the document on masslandrecords.com or your registry's own site, or sign up for the registry's alert service. The law library page points to masslandrecords.com for finding a copy of your deed and mortgage.

It also lists the Secretary of the Commonwealth's registry of deeds consumer notification service, which sends an email whenever a new document is recorded against your property. The Norfolk County registry also keeps a page on deed scams for owners.

Your tax assessor is another record source. The law libraries note that any Massachusetts owner can look up their deed online along with the property record card the assessors use to generate the tax bill.

What other local rules touch a Massachusetts sale?

A few state rules shape the sale beyond recording. Under G.L. c. 93, section 70, an attorney acting for the mortgagee must render a certification of title to the mortgagor and the mortgagee when a purchase money first mortgage is granted on a dwelling for up to four families that the borrower will occupy.

The state's regulation 760 CMR 74 on residential home inspection waivers also matters. It is described by the law library as ensuring that sellers of certain residential properties do not condition acceptance of an offer on a waiver of a home inspection and do not accept offers from buyers who have said they intend to waive one. Whether it reaches your sale depends on the property and the buyer, so ask your attorney.

When a house has liens, back taxes or a muddled chain of title, recording is the step where those problems surface. Raise them with your attorney early.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Massachusetts?

At the registry of deeds for the county or registry district where the property lies. G.L. c. 183, section 4 requires recording there for the deed to be valid against most third parties.

How much is the excise tax when I sell my house?

The tax is a set amount per $500 of the price stated in the deed. The Norfolk County registry states $2.28 per $500 and shows $706.80 on a $155,000 deed, while G.L. c. 64D, section 1 gives a base of $2 per $500. Check your registry for the current rate.

Can a deed be valid but not accepted for recording?

Yes. G.L. c. 183, section 6 says a missing grantee address or consideration recital does not affect validity, but a register of deeds may not accept a deed that lacks them.

Does every Massachusetts property use the same title system?

No. Most properties are recorded land, estimated by the law library at eighty to ninety percent, and the rest are registered land with a Certificate of Title through the Land Court.

Do I need an attorney to record a deed?

The law does not make the owner file personally, but attorneys are a regular part of Massachusetts closings and a lender's closing needs an attorney's substantive involvement under the 2011 Supreme Judicial Court decision cited by the law library.

How do I get a copy of my recorded deed?

Search masslandrecords.com or ask your registry. Norfolk County lists copies at $1.00 per page, plus a postage charge for copies ordered by mail.
